claim: The xlg2 mutant displayed significantly reduced resistance to Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato (Pst).
source: One mutant displayed significantly reduced resistance was xlg2 (Figure 1A), confirming previous report by Zhu et al. (2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and is also supported by citation to Zhu et al. (2009).

claim: The xlg2 mutant is compromised in flg22-induced ROS production.
source: Further characterization indicated that the mutant is compromised in flg22-induced ROS (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), confirming results reported previously (Maruta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and is also supported by citation to Maruta et al. (2015).

claim: XLG2, XLG3, and AGB1, but not XLG1, were induced in response to flg22 treatment.
source: An examination of gene expression showed that XLG2, XLG3, and AGB1, but not XLG1, were induced in response to flg22 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: XLG2/3, but not XLG1, are required for flg22-induced responses and disease resistance to P. syringae.
source: This is in agreement with the recent report that XLG2/3, but not XLG1, are required for flg22-induced responses and disease resistance to P. syringae (Maruta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maruta et al. (2015).

claim: The xlg2 and agb1 mutants were similarly compromised in flg22-induced ROS burst and resistance against Pst.
source: A comparison of xlg2 and agb1 mutant showed that the two mutants were similarly compromised in flg22-induced ROS burst and resistance against Pst, supporting that they act together to regulate FLS2 immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental comparison of mutant phenotypes.

claim: xlg2 plants were more susceptible to Pst than agb1 plants in the absence of flg22 treatment.
source: Interestingly, xlg2 plants were more susceptible to Pst than agb1 plants in the absence of flg22 treatment (Figure 1A), suggesting that XLG2 plays additional role in plant immunity independent of AGB1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and leads to an inference about XLG2's additional role.

claim: XLG2 plays additional role in plant immunity independent of AGB1.
source: Interestingly, xlg2 plants were more susceptible to Pst than agb1 plants in the absence of flg22 treatment (Figure 1A), suggesting that XLG2 plays additional role in plant immunity independent of AGB1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential susceptibility of xlg2 and agb1 mutants to Pst.

claim: The xlg3 mutant was similar to WT in Pst resistance and flg22-induced ROS.
source: As reported previously (Maruta et al., 2015), we found that the xlg3 mutant was similar to WT in Pst resistance and flg22-induced ROS, whereas the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant was slightly more defective in Pst resistance (Figure 1A) and flg22-induced ROS (Figure 1B), indicating that XLG2/3 play additive roles in flg22-induced immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Maruta et al. (2015).

claim: The xlg2 xlg3 double mutant was slightly more defective in Pst resistance and flg22-induced ROS than xlg2 alone.
source: As reported previously (Maruta et al., 2015), we found that the xlg3 mutant was similar to WT in Pst resistance and flg22-induced ROS, whereas the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant was slightly more defective in Pst resistance (Figure 1A) and flg22-induced ROS (Figure 1B), indicating that XLG2/3 play additive roles in flg22-induced immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: XLG2/3 play additive roles in flg22-induced immunity.
source: As reported previously (Maruta et al., 2015), we found that the xlg3 mutant was similar to WT in Pst resistance and flg22-induced ROS, whereas the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant was slightly more defective in Pst resistance (Figure 1A) and flg22-induced ROS (Figure 1B), indicating that XLG2/3 play additive roles in flg22-induced immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the additive phenotype of the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant.

claim: AGG1/2, but not AGG3 and GPA1, are required for flg22-induced defense responses and Pst resistance.
source: Because AGG1/2, but not AGG3 and GPA1, are required for flg22-induced defense responses and Pst resistance (Liu et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013), these results confirmed that the heterotrimeric G proteins required for FLS2 signaling and Pst resistance include the non-canonical Gα proteins XLG2/3, Gβ protein AGB1, and Gγ proteins AGG1/2.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Torres et al., 2013.

claim: The heterotrimeric G proteins required for FLS2 signaling and Pst resistance include the non-canonical Gα proteins XLG2/3, Gβ protein AGB1, and Gγ proteins AGG1/2.
source: Because AGG1/2, but not AGG3 and GPA1, are required for flg22-induced defense responses and Pst resistance (Liu et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013), these results confirmed that the heterotrimeric G proteins required for FLS2 signaling and Pst resistance include the non-canonical Gα proteins XLG2/3, Gβ protein AGB1, and Gγ proteins AGG1/2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: XLG2/3 form heterotrimers with the Gβγ dimer through AGB1.
source: Previous yeast two-hybrid, yeast tri-hybrid and Bi-Fluorescence Complementation assays showed that XLG2/3 form heterotrimers with the Gβγ dimer through AGB1 (Zhu et al., 2009; Maruta et al., 2015; Chakravorty et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2009; Maruta et al., 2015; and Chakravorty et al., 2015.

claim: XLG2 interacts with AGB1 in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants.
source: Consistent with this, luciferase complementation and co-immunoprecipitation assays detected XLG2-AGB1 and XLG3-AGB1 interactions in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: XLG3 interacts with AGB1 in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants.
source: Consistent with this, luciferase complementation and co-immunoprecipitation assays detected XLG2-AGB1 and XLG3-AGB1 interactions in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: XLG2 interacts with AGB1 in Arabidopsis protoplasts.
source: Consistent with this, luciferase complementation and co-immunoprecipitation assays detected XLG2-AGB1 and XLG3-AGB1 interactions in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: XLG3 interacts with AGB1 in Arabidopsis protoplasts.
source: Consistent with this, luciferase complementation and co-immunoprecipitation assays detected XLG2-AGB1 and XLG3-AGB1 interactions in Nicotiana Benthamiana (Nb) plants (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and Arabidopsis protoplasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: Both the N and C termini of XLG2 are sufficient for the interaction with AGB1.
source: Both the N and C termini of XLG2 are sufficient for the interaction with AGB1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: XLG2-FLAG and AGB1-HA retain their biological functions when introduced into agb1 protoplasts or xlg2 plants.
source: Note that XLG2-FLAG and AGB1-HA used in co-IP assays retain their biological functions when introduced into agb1 protoplasts or xlg2 plants (see below in Figures 1D and 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 5E.

claim: Flg22 treatment resulted in a great reduction in XLG2-AGB1 interaction in Nb plants.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the flg22 treatment resulted in a great reduction in XLG2-AGB1 interaction in Nb plants, suggesting that Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins are reminiscent of their animal counterparts in that the heterotrimer is dynamically regulated upon ligand activation of receptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins are reminiscent of their animal counterparts in that the heterotrimer is dynamically regulated upon ligand activation of receptors.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, the flg22 treatment resulted in a great reduction in XLG2-AGB1 interaction in Nb plants, suggesting that Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins are reminiscent of their animal counterparts in that the heterotrimer is dynamically regulated upon ligand activation of receptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the flg22-induced reduction in XLG2-AGB1 interaction and draws on knowledge of animal G protein regulation.

claim: Flg22-induced ROS requires phosphorylation of the NADPH oxidase RbohD by the BIK1 kinase.
source: Because the heterotrimeric G protein mutants under investigation all display defects in flg22-induced ROS, which requires phosphorylation of the NADPH oxidase RbohD by the BIK1 kinase (Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014), we monitored the flg22-induced phosphorylation of RbohD in agb1 using antibodies that recognize the BIK1-specific S39 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kadota et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: Flg22-induced S39 phosphorylation of RbohD was significantly reduced in agb1 mutant protoplasts.
source: Flg22-induced S39 phosphorylation was significantly reduced in agb1 mutant protoplasts, whereas complementation of the mutant protoplasts with AGB1 restored RbohD S39 phosphorylation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Complementation of agb1 mutant protoplasts with AGB1 restored RbohD S39 phosphorylation.
source: Flg22-induced S39 phosphorylation was significantly reduced in agb1 mutant protoplasts, whereas complementation of the mutant protoplasts with AGB1 restored RbohD S39 phosphorylation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Transient overexpression of AGB1 in WT protoplasts resulted in constitutive S39 phosphorylation in RbohD.
source: Consistent with a positive role of AGB1 in flg22-induced RbohD S39 phosphorylation, transient overexpression of AGB1 in WT protoplasts resulted in constitutive S39 phosphorylation in RbohD (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The heterotrimeric G proteins regulate early components of the FLS2 signaling pathway.
source: Together these results suggest that the hetero-trimeric G proteins regulate early components of the FLS2 signaling pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of G protein mutations on RbohD phosphorylation and ROS production.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of XLG2-FLAG immune complex identified four peptides corresponding to PBL20.
source: LC-MS/MS analysis of the immune complex identified four peptides corresponding to PBL20 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), a homolog of BIK1.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of CPR5-FLAG failed to identify any PBL20 peptides.
source: In contrast, immunoprecipitation of the control protein CPR5-FLAG failed to identify any PBL20 peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data from the control experiment.

claim: XLG2/3 interact strongly with PBL20.
source: Co-IP and luciferase complementation assays confirmed that XLG2/3 indeed interacted strongly with PBL20 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: AGB1 interacts with PBL20, albeit much weaker than XLG2.
source: AGB1 also interacted with PBL20, albeit much weaker than did XLG2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing interaction strengths.

claim: PBL20 and BIK1 belong to the same family of receptor like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs) and share similar biochemical properties.
source: Because PBL20 and BIK1 belong to the same family of receptor like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs) and share similar biochemical properties (Zhang et al., 2010), we therefore tested whether BIK1 also interacts with the G proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: XLG2/3 strongly interact with BIK1 but not BAK1 or CPR5 in Nb plants.
source: Luciferase complementation assays showed that XLG2/3 strongly interacted with BIK1 but not BAK1 or CPR5 in Nb plants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), whereas AGB1 interacted with BIK1 at a much lower level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AGB1 interacts with BIK1 at a much lower level than XLG2/3.
source: Luciferase complementation assays showed that XLG2/3 strongly interacted with BIK1 but not BAK1 or CPR5 in Nb plants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), whereas AGB1 interacted with BIK1 at a much lower level.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: FLS2 displays strong interactions with XLG2/3 and a weaker interaction with AGB1.
source: Similarly, FLS2 also displayed strong interactions with XLG2/3 and a weaker interaction with AGB1 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the absence of flg22 treatment, XLG2/3 strongly interact with BIK1 and FLS2.
source: In the absence of flg22 treatment, XLG2/3 strongly interacted with BIK1 and FLS2 (Figure 2B–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Treatment of protoplasts with flg22 led to a much weaker interaction between XLG2 and the FLS2 receptor complex.
source: Treatment of protoplasts with flg22 led to a much weaker interaction, indicating that flg22 induces dissociation of XLG2 from the FLS2 receptor complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced interaction after flg22 treatment.

claim: Flg22 induces dissociation of XLG2 from the FLS2 receptor complex.
source: Treatment of protoplasts with flg22 led to a much weaker interaction, indicating that flg22 induces dissociation of XLG2 from the FLS2 receptor complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced interaction observed after flg22 treatment.

claim: The BIK1K105E mutant protein is defective in ATP-binding and dominantly inhibits flg22-induced signaling when expressed in protoplasts.
source: The BIK1K105E-HA mutant protein, which is defective in ATP-binding and dominantly inhibits flg22-induced signaling when expressed in protoplasts (Zhang et al., 2010), interacted with XLG2 and XLG3 irrespective of the presence or absence of flg22, suggesting that the activation of the BIK1 kinase is required for the dissociation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: BIK1K105E interacts with XLG2 and XLG3 irrespective of the presence or absence of flg22.
source: The BIK1K105E-HA mutant protein, which is defective in ATP-binding and dominantly inhibits flg22-induced signaling when expressed in protoplasts (Zhang et al., 2010), interacted with XLG2 and XLG3 irrespective of the presence or absence of flg22, suggesting that the activation of the BIK1 kinase is required for the dissociation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing constitutive interaction of BIK1K105E with XLG2/3.

claim: The activation of the BIK1 kinase is required for the dissociation of XLG2 from BIK1.
source: The BIK1K105E-HA mutant protein, which is defective in ATP-binding and dominantly inhibits flg22-induced signaling when expressed in protoplasts (Zhang et al., 2010), interacted with XLG2 and XLG3 irrespective of the presence or absence of flg22, suggesting that the activation of the BIK1 kinase is required for the dissociation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the kinase-dead BIK1K105E mutant maintains interaction with XLG2/3 even in the presence of flg22.

claim: The C terminus of XLG2 directly interacts with FLS2 kinase domain.
source: GST pull-down assays showed that the HIS-tagged C-terminal fragment of XLG2 strongly interacted with GST-tagged FLS2 kinase domain, but not GST alone (Figure 2D), indicating that the C terminus of XLG2 directly interacts with FLS2.
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The C terminus of XLG2 interacts strongly with BIK1 and FLS2.
source: Luciferase complementation and Co-IP assays showed that the C terminus of XLG2 interacted strongly with BIK1 and FLS2, whereas the N terminus of XLG2 displayed weak interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C), indicating that XLG2 interacts with FLS2 and BIK1 primarily through its C terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: The N terminus of XLG2 displays weak interactions with BIK1 and FLS2.
source: Luciferase complementation and Co-IP assays showed that the C terminus of XLG2 interacted strongly with BIK1 and FLS2, whereas the N terminus of XLG2 displayed weak interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C), indicating that XLG2 interacts with FLS2 and BIK1 primarily through its C terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: XLG2 interacts with FLS2 and BIK1 primarily through its C terminus.
source: Luciferase complementation and Co-IP assays showed that the C terminus of XLG2 interacted strongly with BIK1 and FLS2, whereas the N terminus of XLG2 displayed weak interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C), indicating that XLG2 interacts with FLS2 and BIK1 primarily through its C terminus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential interaction strengths of XLG2 N and C termini with BIK1 and FLS2.

claim: The C terminus of XLG2 dissociates from BIK1 when protoplasts are treated with flg22.
source: Similar to the full-length XLG2 protein, the C terminus of XLG2 also dissociated from BIK1 when protoplasts were treated with flg22 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: GST pull-down assay showed a weak interaction between XLG2 and BIK1.
source: Surprisingly, GST pull-down assay showed a weak interaction between XLG2 and BIK1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Phosphatase treatment of BIK1 enhanced its interaction with XLG2.
source: Interestingly, phosphatase treatment of BIK1 enhanced its interaction with XLG2 (Figure 2E), suggesting that XLG2 has greater affinity with non-phosphorylated BIK1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: XLG2 has greater affinity with non-phosphorylated BIK1.
source: Interestingly, phosphatase treatment of BIK1 enhanced its interaction with XLG2 (Figure 2E), suggesting that XLG2 has greater affinity with non-phosphorylated BIK1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced interaction between XLG2 and dephosphorylated BIK1.

claim: The de-phosphorylated form of BIK1 strongly interacts with AGB1.
source: While the un-treated BIK1 is unable to interact with AGB1, the de-phosphorylated form of BIK1 strongly interacted with AGB1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The un-treated BIK1 is unable to interact with AGB1.
source: While the un-treated BIK1 is unable to interact with AGB1, the de-phosphorylated form of BIK1 strongly interacted with AGB1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The G proteins dynamically interact with the FLS2-BIK1 receptor complex during FLS2 signaling.
source: Together the results show that the G proteins dynamically interact with the FLS2-BIK1 receptor complex during FLS2 signaling, and the findings are consistent with the observed defects in flg22-induced responses and RbohD phosphorylation in the G protein mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing flg22-regulated interactions.

claim: AGB1 is required for accumulation of BIK1, but not FLS2 and BAK1.
source: Immunoblot analyses showed that the BIK1-HA protein accumulated to a much lower level in agb1 compared to WT (Figure 3A), indicating that AGB1 is required for BIK1 accumulation in plants. In contrast, FLS2 and BAK1 protein accumulation was not affected in agb1, indicating a specific effect on BIK1 protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The BIK1-HA transgene is similarly expressed in agb1 and WT plants.
source: Examination of BIK1-HA transcripts indicated that the transgene is similarly expressed in agb1 and WT plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcript analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A much lower BIK1-HA accumulation was observed in agb1 than in WT plants when BIK1-HA is expressed under the 35S promoter.
source: To further rule out the possibility that AGB1 modulates BIK1 at transcriptional level, we transformed agb1 and WT plants with BIK1-HA transgene under the control of the 35S promoter. Again, a much lower BIK1-HA accumulation was observed in agb1 than in WT plants although the BIK1-HA transcripts accumulated to similar levels in the two lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The BIK1-HA protein accumulation was greatly reduced in agg1 agg2 double mutant plants.
source: Similarly, the BIK1-HA protein accumulation was greatly reduced in agg1 agg2 double mutant plants (Figure 3B), indicating that AGG1/2 are also required for BIK1 accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AGG1/2 are required for BIK1 accumulation.
source: Similarly, the BIK1-HA protein accumulation was greatly reduced in agg1 agg2 double mutant plants (Figure 3B), indicating that AGG1/2 are also required for BIK1 accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced BIK1 accumulation in agg1 agg2 mutants.

claim: BIK1 accumulated to lower levels in the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant than in WT protoplasts.
source: We further asked whether XLG2 and XLG3 are required for BIK1 accumulation by transiently expressing BIK1-HA in xlg2 xlg3 mutant protoplasts. Regardless of the promoter used for BIK1-HA expression, BIK1 accumulated to lower levels in the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant than in WT protoplasts (Figure 3C), indicating that XLG2/3 are also required for BIK1 accumulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: XLG2/3 are required for BIK1 accumulation.
source: We further asked whether XLG2 and XLG3 are required for BIK1 accumulation by transiently expressing BIK1-HA in xlg2 xlg3 mutant protoplasts. Regardless of the promoter used for BIK1-HA expression, BIK1 accumulated to lower levels in the xlg2 xlg3 double mutant than in WT protoplasts (Figure 3C), indicating that XLG2/3 are also required for BIK1 accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced BIK1 accumulation in xlg2 xlg3 mutants.

claim: The defect in protein accumulation is specific to BIK1, as BAK1 accumulation was not affected in xlg2 xlg3 protoplasts.
source: The defect in protein accumulation is specific to BIK1, as BAK1 accumulation was not affected in xlg2 xlg3 protoplasts (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The accumulation of BIK1-HA was not affected in gpa1 mutant plants.
source: The accumulation of BIK1-HA was not affected in gpa1 mutant plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), a result that is consistent with previous report that GPA1 is not required for flg22-induced ROS (Liu et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GPA1 is not required for flg22-induced ROS.
source: The accumulation of BIK1-HA was not affected in gpa1 mutant plants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), a result that is consistent with previous report that GPA1 is not required for flg22-induced ROS (Liu et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Torres et al., 2013.

claim: BIK1 is turned-over through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.
source: BIK1 is known to be turned-over through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (Monaghan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Monaghan et al., 2014.

claim: Treatment of plants with proteasome inhibitors PS341 and MG132 restored BIK1 accumulation in agb1 mutant plants.
source: Treatment of plants with proteasome inhibitors PS341 (Figure 3D) and MG132 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) restored BIK1 accumulation in agb1 mutant plants, suggesting that AGB1 regulates BIK1 stability through the proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AGB1 regulates BIK1 stability through the proteasome pathway.
source: Treatment of plants with proteasome inhibitors PS341 (Figure 3D) and MG132 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) restored BIK1 accumulation in agb1 mutant plants, suggesting that AGB1 regulates BIK1 stability through the proteasome pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the restoration of BIK1 accumulation by proteasome inhibitors in agb1 mutants.

claim: The recombinant BIK1 was degraded in the WT extract, and this degradation was blocked by PS341.
source: The recombinant BIK1 was degraded in the WT extract, and this degradation was blocked by PS341 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), recapitulating the proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1 in plants.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The rate of BIK1 degradation was more rapid in agb1 and xlg2 xlg3 extracts compared to that in the WT extract.
source: The rate of BIK1 degradation was more rapid in agb1 and xlg2 xlg3 extracts compared to that in the WT extract (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: PBL20 was degraded in WT extracts, and this degradation was enhanced when extracts from xlg2 xlg3 or agb1 mutants were used.
source: Indeed, PBL20 was also degraded in WT extracts, and this degradation was enhanced when extracts from xlg2 xlg3 or agb1 mutants were used (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: The heterotrimeric G proteins formed by XLG2/3, AGB1, and AGG1/2 attenuate proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1 and PBL20.
source: Together these results demonstrate that the heterotrimeric G proteins formed by XLG2/3, AGB1, and AGG1/2 attenuate proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1 and PBL20.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing enhanced degradation of BIK1 and PBL20 in G protein mutants.

claim: Transient overexpression of BIK1 in xlg2 xlg3 and agb1 protoplasts largely restored the flg22-induced RbohD S39 phosphorylation.
source: Transient overexpression of BIK1 in xlg2 xlg3 and agb1 protoplasts largely restored the flg22-induced RbohD S39 phosphorylation (Figure 4A), indicating that the heterotrimeric G proteins positively regulate RbohD phosphorylation at least in part by enhancing BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The heterotrimeric G proteins positively regulate RbohD phosphorylation at least in part by enhancing BIK1 stability.
source: Transient overexpression of BIK1 in xlg2 xlg3 and agb1 protoplasts largely restored the flg22-induced RbohD S39 phosphorylation (Figure 4A), indicating that the heterotrimeric G proteins positively regulate RbohD phosphorylation at least in part by enhancing BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the restoration of RbohD phosphorylation by BIK1 overexpression in G protein mutants.

claim: Introgression of the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into agb1 significantly enhanced flg22-induced ROS production compared to agb1 plants with only endogenous BIK1.
source: Introgression of the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into agb1 by crossing significantly enhanced flg22-induced ROS production in these plants compared to agb1 plants that contained only the endogenous copy of BIK1 (Figure 4B), indicating that increasing BIK1 accumulation by the transgene at least partially restored flg22-induced ROS in agb1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increasing BIK1 accumulation by the transgene at least partially restored flg22-induced ROS in agb1.
source: Introgression of the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into agb1 by crossing significantly enhanced flg22-induced ROS production in these plants compared to agb1 plants that contained only the endogenous copy of BIK1 (Figure 4B), indicating that increasing BIK1 accumulation by the transgene at least partially restored flg22-induced ROS in agb1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced ROS production in agb1 plants carrying the BIK1 transgene.

claim: Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants displayed higher level of ROS compared to non-transgenic WT plants.
source: Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants displayed higher level of ROS compared to non-transgenic WT plants (Figure 4B), indicating that BIK1 protein level is rate-limiting in flg22-induced immune responses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BIK1 protein level is rate-limiting in flg22-induced immune responses.
source: Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants displayed higher level of ROS compared to non-transgenic WT plants (Figure 4B), indicating that BIK1 protein level is rate-limiting in flg22-induced immune responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the enhanced ROS production in plants with increased BIK1 levels.

claim: The agb1 NP::BIK1-HA plants were indistinguishable from WT in flg22-induced resistance to Pst.
source: While the agb1 consistently supported greater amount of bacterial growth compared to WT plants following flg22 treatment, the agb1 NP::BIK1-HA plants were indistinguishable from WT (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants supported less bacterial growth than WT plants.
source: Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants supported less bacterial growth than did WT plants, further supporting the importance of BIK1 abundance in FLS2-mediated immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced bacterial growth in Col-0 NP::BIK1-HA plants.

claim: xlg2 xlg3 transgenic lines carrying the NP::BIK1-HA transgene displayed near WT ROS production.
source: We similarly introduced the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into xlg2 xlg3 double mutant plants by transformation. The resulting transgenic lines displayed near WT ROS production (Figure 4D) and Pst resistance (Figure 4E) in response to flg22 treatment, indicating that XLG2/3 also regulate FLS2-mediated immunity by controlling BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: xlg2 xlg3 transgenic lines carrying the NP::BIK1-HA transgene displayed near WT Pst resistance.
source: We similarly introduced the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into xlg2 xlg3 double mutant plants by transformation. The resulting transgenic lines displayed near WT ROS production (Figure 4D) and Pst resistance (Figure 4E) in response to flg22 treatment, indicating that XLG2/3 also regulate FLS2-mediated immunity by controlling BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: XLG2/3 regulate FLS2-mediated immunity by controlling BIK1 stability.
source: We similarly introduced the NP::BIK1-HA transgene into xlg2 xlg3 double mutant plants by transformation. The resulting transgenic lines displayed near WT ROS production (Figure 4D) and Pst resistance (Figure 4E) in response to flg22 treatment, indicating that XLG2/3 also regulate FLS2-mediated immunity by controlling BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the restoration of immune responses in xlg2 xlg3 mutants by the BIK1 transgene.

claim: An examination of XLG2 N-terminal fragment expressed in protoplasts following flg22 treatment showed a prominent shift in protein migration in SDS-PAGE.
source: An examination of XLG2 N-terminal fragment expressed in protoplasts following flg22 treatment showed a prominent shift in protein migration in SDS-PAGE (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The shift of XLG2 protein mobility was sensitive to phosphatase treatment, which is indicative of flg22-induced phosphorylation in XLG2.
source: The shift of protein mobility was sensitive to phosphatase treatment, which is indicative of flg22-induced phosphorylation in XLG2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing phosphatase-sensitive mobility shift.

claim: The flg22-induced phosphorylation similarly occurred to the N terminus of XLG3, but not XLG1.
source: The flg22-induced phosphorylation similarly occurred to the N terminus of XLG3, but not XLG1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the notion that XLG2/3 but not XLG1, are involved in flg22 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis of XLG2-FLAG identified 23 phospho-peptides corresponding to at least 15 phospho-sites.
source: To determine phospho-sites in XLG2, we expressed full-length XLG2-FLAG in protoplasts. Following flg22 treatment, the XLG2-FLAG protein was affinity-purified and subject to LC-MS/MS analysis for phospho-peptides. We were able to recover 87% of total peptide sequence, among which we identified 23 phospho-peptides corresponding to at least 15 phospho-sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: All but two phospho-peptides in XLG2 were located in the N terminus.
source: Interestingly, all but two phospho-peptides were located in the N terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: Phospho-sites between amino acids 141–156 in XLG2 accounted for nearly half of the phospho-peptides.
source: Strikingly, phospho-sites between amino acids 141–156 accounted for nearly half of the phospho-peptides.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claim: Amino acids Ser141, Ser148, Ser150 and Ser151 are required for overall phosphorylation of XLG2 in response to flg22 treatment.
source: We further tested whether these are the major phospho-sites by site-directed mutagenesis. Simultaneously substituting three to four of these residues into non-phosphorylatable alanine (XLG2S148A,S150A,S151A; XLG2S141A,S148A,S150A,S151A) resulted in severe reduction to complete elimination in flg22-induced band shift in XLG2 N terminus (Figure 5B), indicating that amino acids Ser141, Ser148, Ser150 and Ser151 are indeed required for overall phosphorylation of XLG2 in response to flg22 treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by site-directed mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BIK1 phosphorylates XLG2 N terminus in vitro.
source: We next tested whether BIK1 is able to phosphorylate XLG2 N terminus in vitro Radio-labelling assay showed that the recombinant BIK1, but not BIK1K105E, strongly phosphorylated the N terminus of XLG2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: S148 and S150 in XLG2 were phosphorylated in vitro by BIK1, but not BIK1K105E.
source: To determine whether the major phospho-sites in XLG2 were also phosphorylated by BIK1, we raised antibodies that specifically recognize phospho-S148 and phospho-S150. Immunoblot analysis showed that S148 and S150 were indeed phosphorylated in vitro by BIK1, but not BIK1K105E (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: xlg2 transgenic lines carrying the WT or phospho-mimicking XLG2-FLAG transgene completely restored the flg22-induced ROS to WT level.
source: We introduced WT, non-phosphorylatable (XLG2S141A,S148A,S150A,S151A) and phospho-mimicking (XLG2S141D,S148D,S150D,S151D) forms of XLG2-FLAG transgene under control of the native XLG2 promoter into xlg2 plants and analyzed flg22-induced ROS production in the resulting transgenic lines. While the xlg2 transgenic lines carrying the WT or phospho-mimicking XLG2-FLAG transgene completely restored the flg22-induced ROS to WT level, the two lines transformed with the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene only partially restored the flg22-induced ROS (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: xlg2 transgenic lines carrying the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene only partially restored the flg22-induced ROS.
source: We introduced WT, non-phosphorylatable (XLG2S141A,S148A,S150A,S151A) and phospho-mimicking (XLG2S141D,S148D,S150D,S151D) forms of XLG2-FLAG transgene under control of the native XLG2 promoter into xlg2 plants and analyzed flg22-induced ROS production in the resulting transgenic lines. While the xlg2 transgenic lines carrying the WT or phospho-mimicking XLG2-FLAG transgene completely restored the flg22-induced ROS to WT level, the two lines transformed with the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene only partially restored the flg22-induced ROS (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The phosphorylation of XLG2 is required, but not sufficient, for optimum activation of RbohD.
source: The inability of phospho-mimicking XLG2 to constitutively activate ROS suggests that the phosphorylation of XLG2 is required, but not sufficient, for optimum activation of RbohD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that phospho-mimicking XLG2 does not constitutively activate ROS.

claim: xlg2/3 transgenic lines carrying the WT XLG2-FLAG transgene were fully restored in resistance to Pst.
source: We further introduced WT and the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene into xlg2/3 double mutants, and inoculated independent lines with Pst. While the line carrying the WT XLG2-FLAG transgene was fully restored in resistance to Pst that was indistinguishable from the WT non-transgenic plants, the two lines transformed with the non-phosphorylatable XLG-FLAG transgene were only marginally more resistant to Pst (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: xlg2/3 transgenic lines carrying the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene were only marginally more resistant to Pst.
source: We further introduced WT and the non-phosphorylatable XLG2-FLAG transgene into xlg2/3 double mutants, and inoculated independent lines with Pst. While the line carrying the WT XLG2-FLAG transgene was fully restored in resistance to Pst that was indistinguishable from the WT non-transgenic plants, the two lines transformed with the non-phosphorylatable XLG-FLAG transgene were only marginally more resistant to Pst (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The phosphorylation of XLG2 is required, but not sufficient, for full function of XLG2.
source: These results indicated that the phosphorylation is required, but not sufficient, for full function of XLG2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the partial restoration of function by non-phosphorylatable XLG2 and lack of constitutive activation by phospho-mimicking XLG2.

claim: The phospho-site mutants of XLG2 allowed similar BIK1-HA accumulation compared to protoplasts expressing the WT XLG2 protein.
source: We next asked whether the phospho-site mutants affect BIK1 stability or XLG2-BIK1 interaction. When expressed in protoplasts isolated from xlg2 xlg3 plants, the phospho-site mutants allowed similar BIK1-HA accumulation compared to protoplasts expressing the WT XLG2 protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phospho-site mutants of XLG2 showed normal interaction with BIK1 in the absence of flg22 and normal dissociation from BIK1 in the presence of flg22.
source: These mutants also showed normal interaction with BIK1 in the absence of flg22 and normal dissociation from BIK1 in the presence of flg22.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing normal interaction dynamics.

claim: The phosphorylation of XLG2 phospho-sites affected neither BIK1 stability nor interaction with BIK1.
source: The results suggest that the phosphorylation of these sites affected neither BIK1 stability nor interaction with BIK1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal BIK1 accumulation and interaction in the presence of phospho-site mutants.

claim: XLG2 interacts strongly with RbohD in Arabidopsis plants.
source: Indeed, XLG2 interacted strongly with RbohD in Arabidopsis plants (Figure 5G) and Nb plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), providing an explanation that XLG2 phosphorylation regulates ROS burst independent of BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: XLG2 interacts strongly with RbohD in Nb plants.
source: Indeed, XLG2 interacted strongly with RbohD in Arabidopsis plants (Figure 5G) and Nb plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), providing an explanation that XLG2 phosphorylation regulates ROS burst independent of BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: XLG2 phosphorylation regulates ROS burst independent of BIK1 stability.
source: Indeed, XLG2 interacted strongly with RbohD in Arabidopsis plants (Figure 5G) and Nb plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), providing an explanation that XLG2 phosphorylation regulates ROS burst independent of BIK1 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the XLG2-RbohD interaction and the observation that phospho-site mutations affect ROS but not BIK1 stability.

claim: The XLG2-RbohD interaction was detected in the absence of flg22 treatment.
source: The XLG2-RbohD interaction was detected in the absence of flg22 treatment, indicating that the XLG2 constitutively interacts with RbohD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing interaction without flg22 treatment.

claim: XLG2 constitutively interacts with RbohD.
source: The XLG2-RbohD interaction was detected in the absence of flg22 treatment, indicating that the XLG2 constitutively interacts with RbohD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of XLG2-RbohD interaction in the absence of flg22.

claim: The Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins positively regulate plant immunity by directly interacting with the FLS2-BIK1 immune receptor complex.
source: In this study we show that the Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins positively regulate plant immunity by directly interacting with the FLS2-BIK1 immune receptor complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Before activation, XLG2/3, AGB1, and AGG1/2 positively regulate BIK1 stability by attenuating proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1.
source: The heterotrimeric G proteins regulate FLS2-mediated immunity through at least two mechanisms. Before activation, XLG2/3, AGB1, and AGG1/2 positively regulate BIK1 stability by attenuating proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enhanced BIK1 degradation in G protein mutants.

claim: Upon activation of the FLS2-BIK1 complex by flg22, BIK1 directly phosphorylates XLG2 in the N terminus to regulate flg22-induced ROS production.
source: Upon activation of the FLS2-BIK1 complex by flg22, BIK1 directly phosphorylates XLG2 in the N terminus to regulate flg22-induced ROS production, likely through the XLG2-RbohD interaction (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing BIK1-mediated phosphorylation of XLG2 and its effect on ROS production.

claim: The maize Gα protein CT2 interacts with the receptor kinase CLV1 to control shoot meristem development.
source: The maize Gα protein CT2 interacts with the receptor kinase CLV1 to control shoot meristem development (Bommert et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bommert et al., 2013.

claim: GPA1 and AGG1/2 interact with BAK1 and CERK1 in yeast two-hybrid and Bi-Fluorescence Complementation assays.
source: GPA1 and AGG1/2 have been shown to interact with BAK1 and CERK1 in yeast two-hybrid and Bi-Fluorescence Complementation assays, although the biological significance of this remains unknown (Aranda-Sicilia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aranda-Sicilia et al., 2015.

claim: Plant receptor kinases fulfil the roles of GPCRs by directly coupling to heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: Thus, these studies collectively support that plant receptor kinases fulfil the roles of GPCRs by directly coupling to heterotrimeric G proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective evidence of receptor kinase-G protein interactions in plants.

claim: The G proteins coupled to the FLS2 receptor complex are subject to multiple regulations during FLS2 signaling.
source: Importantly, we show that the G proteins coupled to the FLS2 receptor complex are subject to multiple regulations during FLS2 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dynamic regulation of G protein interactions.

claim: The flg22-induced dissociation of XLG2 from AGB1 likely reflects an increase of GTP-bound form of Gα which dissociates from the Gβγ dimer upon receptor activation.
source: The flg22-induced dissociation of XLG2 from AGB1 likely reflects an increase of GTP-bound form of Gα which dissociates from the Gβγ dimer upon receptor activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed flg22-induced dissociation and knowledge of G protein activation mechanisms.

claim: The flg22-induced dissociation of the G proteins from BIK1 coincides with the flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation.
source: The flg22-induced dissociation of the G proteins from BIK1 coincides with the flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation, suggesting that the flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation triggers the dissociation of the G proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of temporal correlation.

claim: The flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation triggers the dissociation of the G proteins.
source: The flg22-induced dissociation of the G proteins from BIK1 coincides with the flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation, suggesting that the flg22-induced BIK1 phosphorylation triggers the dissociation of the G proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation and the observation that kinase-dead BIK1 maintains interaction.

claim: De-phosphorylation of BIK1 strongly enhanced its interactions with both XLG2 and AGB1 in vitro.
source: Indeed, de-phosphorylation of BIK1 strongly enhanced its interactions with both XLG2 and AGB1 in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro interaction assay data.

claim: The decoupling of the G proteins from the receptor may be necessary for the regulation of down-stream effectors.
source: The decoupling of the G proteins from the receptor maybe necessary for the regulation of down-stream effectors.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed dissociation dynamics.

claim: BIK1 is subject to proteasome-dependent degradation.
source: BIK1 is subject to proteasome-dependent degradation (Monaghan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Monaghan et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of XLG2 and AGB1 leads to accelerated degradation of BIK1.
source: Loss of XLG2 and AGB1 leads to accelerated degradation of BIK1, and this is blocked by the addition of proteasome inhibitors, indicating that the G proteins attenuating the proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing accelerated BIK1 degradation in mutants.

claim: The G proteins attenuate the proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1.
source: Loss of XLG2 and AGB1 leads to accelerated degradation of BIK1, and this is blocked by the addition of proteasome inhibitors, indicating that the G proteins attenuating the proteasome-dependent degradation of BIK1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the accelerated degradation in mutants and rescue by proteasome inhibitors.

claim: FLS2 is subject to proteasome-dependent degradation.
source: FLS2 is also subject to proteasome-dependent degradation (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2011.

claim: FLS2 accumulation is not affected by the agb1 mutation.
source: However, FLS2 accumulation is not affected by the agb1 mutation, indicating that the G proteins do not generally regulate proteasome-mediated protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing normal FLS2 levels in agb1.

claim: The G proteins do not generally regulate proteasome-mediated protein degradation.
source: However, FLS2 accumulation is not affected by the agb1 mutation, indicating that the G proteins do not generally regulate proteasome-mediated protein degradation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the selective effect on BIK1 but not FLS2 degradation.

claim: A major function of the heterotrimeric G protein is to maintain the signaling competence of the FLS2-BIK1 complex in the pre-activation state.
source: Importantly, introduction of a transgenic copy of BIK1 largely restored flg22-triggered immune responses and disease resistance in xlg2 and agb1 mutants, demonstrating that a major function of the heterotrimeric G protein is to maintain the signaling competence of the FLS2-BIK1 complex in the pre-activation state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the restoration of immune responses by BIK1 transgene in G protein mutants.

claim: Flg22 induces the phosphorylation of XLG2 in the N terminus.
source: In addition to the ligand-induced dissociation of XLG2 from AGB1, flg22 induces the phosphorylation of XLG2 in the N terminus.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation-induced mobility shift.

claim: The phosphorylation of XLG2 is likely caused by the BIK1 family kinases.
source: This phosphorylation is likely caused by the BIK1 family kinases, as two of the major phosphor-sites induced by flg22 are also phosphorylated by BIK1 in vitro.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro phosphorylation of XLG2 by BIK1 and the overlap of phospho-sites.

claim: Non-phosphorylatable XLG2 mutants are compromised in flg22-induced ROS production and disease resistance to Pst.
source: Non-phosphorylatable XLG2 mutants are compromised in flg22-induced ROS production and disease resistance to Pst, indicating that the phosphorylation plays a positive role.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced ROS and Pst resistance in non-phosphorylatable mutants.

claim: The phosphorylation of XLG2 plays a positive role in flg22-induced ROS production and disease resistance.
source: Non-phosphorylatable XLG2 mutants are compromised in flg22-induced ROS production and disease resistance to Pst, indicating that the phosphorylation plays a positive role.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the compromised phenotype of non-phosphorylatable mutants.

claim: The phosphorylated XLG2 regulates components other than BIK1.
source: However, mutations in the phospho-sites did not affect XLG2-BIK1 interaction nor BIK1 stability, suggesting that the phosphorylated XLG2 regulates components other than BIK1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of phospho-site mutations on BIK1 stability and interaction.

claim: The phosphorylated XLG2 further enhances ROS production by modulating RbohD.
source: Indeed, XLG2 constitutively interacts with RbohD, suggesting that the phosphorylated XLG2 further enhances ROS production by modulating RbohD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the XLG2-RbohD interaction and the effect of XLG2 phosphorylation on ROS.

claim: RbohD is subject to multiple regulations including phosphorylation by CPK5 and BIK1 and calcium binding to EF-hand.
source: RbohD is known to be subject to multiple regulations including phosphorylation by CPK5 and BIK1 (Dubiella et al., 2013; Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014) and calcium binding to EF-hand (Ogasawara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dubiella et al., 2013; Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; and Ogasawara et al., 2008.

claim: RbohD is additionally regulated by a phosphorylated XLG2.
source: The results presented here show that RbohD is additionally regulated by a phosphorylated XLG2, although the underlying mechanism remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of XLG2 phosphorylation on ROS production.

claim: The Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins are analogous to the animal counterpart in that, upon activation by receptors, dissociate from each other and activate downstream effectors.
source: The Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins reported here are analogous to the animal counterpart in that, upon activation by receptors, dissociate from each other and activate downstream effectors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing ligand-induced dissociation and draws on knowledge of animal G protein function.

claim: Unlike the animal heterotrimeric G proteins, the Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins additionally regulate signaling competence of the FLS2-BIK1 complex prior to receptor activation.
source: Unlike the animal heterotrimeric G proteins, however, the Arabidopsis heterotrimeric G proteins additionally regulate signaling competence of the FLS2-BIK1 complex prior to receptor activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing G protein regulation of BIK1 stability before activation.

claim: FLS2 serves as an excellent model for understanding plant innate immune signaling and receptor kinases in general.
source: As an intensely studied Pattern Recognition Receptor (PRR) in plants, FLS2 serves as an excellent model understanding plant innate immune signaling and receptor kinases in general (Macho and Zipfel, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Macho and Zipfel, 2014.

claim: FLS2 forms a dynamic complex with the co-receptor BAK1 and the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1 to perceive flg22 and activate defense responses.
source: It forms a dynamic complex with the co-receptor BAK1 and the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1 to perceive a conserved bacterial flagellar epitope, flg22, to activate a variety of defense responses (Chinchilla et al., 2007; Heese et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chinchilla et al., 2007; Heese et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2010; and Sun et al., 2013.

claim: Stability of FLS2 and BIK1 is subject to regulation by ubiquitin-proteasome system and a calcium-dependent protein kinase.
source: Stability of FLS2 and BIK1 is subject to regulation by ubiquitin-proteasome system and a calcium-dependent protein kinase (Lu et al., 2011; Monaghan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lu et al., 2011 and Monaghan et al., 2014.

claim: BIK1 directly phosphorylates the NADPH oxidase RbohD to prime flg22-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: We and others previously showed that BIK1 directly phosphorylates the NADPH oxidase RbohD to prime flg22-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS; Kadota et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kadota et al., 2014 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: In the pre-activation state, the GDP-bound Gα interacts with the Gβγ dimer to form a heterotrimer in animals.
source: In the pre-activation state, the GDP-bound Gα interacts with the Gβγ dimer to form a heterotrimer.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge of animal G protein function.

claim: Upon activation by GPCR, Gα exchanges GDP for GTP, resulting in the activation of the heterotrimer in animals.
source: Upon activation by GPCR, Gα exchanges GDP for GTP, resulting in the activation of the heterotrimer.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge of animal G protein activation.

claim: The activated Gα and Gβγ dissociate from each other to regulate downstream effectors in animals.
source: The activated Gα and Gβγ dissociate from each other to regulate downstream effectors.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge of animal G protein signaling.

claim: Plants contain canonical Gα (encoded by GPA1 in Arabidopsis), Gβ (encoded by AGB1 in Arabidopsis), Gγ proteins (encoded by AGG1, AGG2), and a non-canonical Gγ (encoded by AGG3 in Arabidopsis).
source: Plants contain canonical Gα (encoded by GPA1 in Arabidopsis), Gβ (encoded by AGB1 in Arabidopsis), Gγ proteins (encoded by AGG1, AGG2), and a non-canonical Gγ (encoded by AGG3 in Arabidopsis) (Urano and Jones, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Urano and Jones, 2013.

claim: Plants additionally encode extra-large G proteins (XLGs, encoded by XLG1, XLG2, and XLG3 in Arabidopsis) that carry a variable N-terminal domain and a C-terminal Gα domain.
source: Plants additionally encode extra-large G proteins (XLGs, encoded by XLG1, XLG2, and XLG3 in Arabidopsis) that carry a variable N-terminal domain and a C-terminal Gα domain (Lee and Assman, 1999; Ding et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee and Assman, 1999 and Ding et al., 2008.

claim: The Arabidopsis XLGs are functional Gα proteins and interact with Gβγ dimers to form heterotrimers.
source: Recent advances indicate that the Arabidopsis XLGs are functional Gα proteins and interact with Gβγ dimers to form heterotrimers (Zhu et al., 2009; Maruta et al., 2015; Chakravorty et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2009; Maruta et al., 2015; and Chakravorty et al., 2015.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins play important roles in a variety of biological processes in plants, including cell division, meristem maintenance, root morphogenesis, seed development and germination, nitrogen assimilation, and response to ABA, low temperature, and blue light.
source: Heterotrimeric G proteins play important roles in a variety of biological processes in plants, including cell division (Ullah et al., 2001, 2003; Chen et al., 2003), meristem maintenance (Bommert et al., 2013), root morphogenesis (Ding et al., 2008), seed development and germination (Chen et al., 2006; Pandey et al., 2006), nitrogen assimilation (Sun et al., 2014), and response to ABA (Wang et al., 2001), low temperature (Ma et al., 2015), and blue light (Warpeha et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to various studies.

claim: Heterotrimeric G proteins play an important role in plant disease resistance against diverse pathogens.
source: Accumulating evidence indicate that heterotrimeric G proteins also play an important role in plant disease resistance against diverse pathogens (Llorente et al., 2005; Trusov et al., 2006; Zhu et al, 2009; Ishikawa, 2009; Cheng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Llorente et al., 2005; Trusov et al., 2006; Zhu et al, 2009; Ishikawa, 2009; and Cheng et al., 2015.

claim: XLG2, AGB1, and AGG1/2 mediate immune responses downstream of PRRs.
source: Recent reports indicate that XLG2, AGB1, and AGG1/2 mediate immune responses downstream of PRRs (Ishikawa, 2009; Zhu et al, 2009; Liu et al., 2013; Lorek et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013; Maruta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: XLG2 plays an important role in basal resistance to P. syringae.
source: XLG2 was first shown to play an important role in basal resistance to P. syringae (Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2009.

claim: XLG2, but not XLG1, is required for resistance to P. syringae and flg22-induced ROS production.
source: A recent report showed that XLG2, but not XLG1, is required for resistance to P. syringae and flg22-induced ROS production (Maruta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maruta et al., 2015.

claim: AGB1 and AGG1/2, but not AGG3, are required for resistance to P. syringae and microbial pattern-induced ROS production.
source: AGB1 and AGG1/2, but not AGG3, are required for resistance to P. syringae and microbial pattern-induced ROS production (Liu et al., 2013; Lorek et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013; Lorek et al., 2013; and Torres et al., 2013.

claim: Epistatic analyses indicated that AGB1 acts in the same pathway as RbohD.
source: Furthermore, epistatic analyses indicated that AGB1 acts in the same pathway as RbohD (Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Torres et al., 2013.

claim: It is still debated whether plants possess 7 transmembrane GPCRs.
source: However, it is still debated whether plants possess 7 transmembrane GPCRs (Taddese et al., 2014; Urano and Jones, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taddese et al., 2014 and Urano and Jones, 2014.

claim: GPA1, AGG1/2 can interact with BAK1 and the chitin-binding receptor kinase CERK1, but not FLS2.
source: One recent report suggests that GPA1, AGG1/2 can interact with BAK1 and the chitin-binding receptor kinase CERK1, but not FLS2 (Aranda-Sicilia et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aranda-Sicilia et al., 2015.

claim: GPA1 does not appear to play a role in flg22-induced ROS and disease resistance to P. syringae.
source: However, GPA1 does not appear to play a role in flg22-induced ROS and disease resistance to P. syringae (Liu et al., 2013; Torres et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2013 and Torres et al., 2013.
